common_name: Karakılçık Wheat (Black-Awned Anatolian Bread Wheat Landrace)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill seed in mid-to-late fall across the Western Black Sea and Central Anatolian highlands where this landrace is traditionally grown, allowing plants to establish a rosette before winter dormancy and resume growth as the ground warms in spring.

directions: Karakılçık is a tall, black-bearded bread wheat landrace long grown as a rainfed winter cereal in the Kastamonu and Çorum provinces of Turkey's Western Black Sea region, where the name translates roughly to 'black awn' for its dark, bristling seed heads. Smallholders traditionally broadcast seed by hand into tilled ground in autumn and rely on stored soil moisture and winter precipitation rather than irrigation, since the landrace has been selected over generations for resilience on marginal upland fields rather than high yield. Its coarse, flavorful grain is prized for tarhana, bulgur, and sourdough-style breads, and a recent wave of chef- and agronomist-driven revival efforts has brought it back into specialty flour mills after decades of decline in favor of higher-yielding semi-dwarf varieties. Because the straw grows tall and lodges more readily than modern cultivars, it performs best on lean soil without heavy nitrogen fertilization.
sources: Morgounov et al., 'Wheat Landraces Currently Grown in Turkey: Distribution, Diversity, and Use', Crop Science, 2016
Republic of Turkey Bahri Dağdaş International Agricultural Research Institute — Wheat Landraces Inventory of Turkey

common_name: Gemlik Olive (Turkish PDO Black Table Olive)

planting.note: Plant grafted or container trees in early spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Gemlik is partially self-fertile but sets a heavier crop with a compatible second cultivar flowering nearby.

directions: Gemlik is Turkey's most widely planted and best-known olive cultivar, named for the Bursa province town on the Sea of Marmara where it has been grown for generations and later received protected-designation-of-origin status for its region-specific character. Fruit is small to medium, round, and thin-skinned with a high oil content, but growers harvest it mainly for brine-cured black table olives rather than pressing, since the thin skin and small pit give an easy-eating texture after a multi-month salt-brine fermentation. Plant in well-drained, low-fertility soil in full sun and avoid overwatering once established, as Gemlik tolerates the hot, dry Mediterranean-type summers of its native Marmara coast better than consistently wet conditions. Harvest fruit as it darkens toward full black ripeness in late fall for the classic sweet, creamy-finished brined olive the cultivar is known for.
sources: Turkish Patent and Trademark Office — Gemlik Zeytini geographical indication registration
Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations — olive germplasm and cultivar records

planting.note: Plant individual cloves 1-2 inches deep in fall in the Black Sea foothills' heavy, mineral-rich soils that Taşköprü is traditionally grown in, giving roots time to establish before winter chilling triggers bulb division in spring.

directions: Taşköprü is a strong-flavored garlic landrace grown around the Taşköprü district of Kastamonu province in Turkey's Black Sea region, where it is nicknamed 'white gold' for its outsized importance to the local farm economy and was granted European Union protected geographical indication status in 2021. Researchers have traced its distinctively pungent, long-lasting aroma to a particular profile of volatile organosulfur compounds that differs measurably from garlic grown even a short distance away, a difference local growers attribute to the district's specific mineral-rich soil and microclimate. Plant cloves pointed-end-up in well-drained soil in autumn and allow the crop a long, cool growing season through winter and spring, since Taşköprü is slower to mature than many commercial softneck types. Harvest once the lower leaves yellow, then cure bulbs in a warm, dry, shaded spot for several weeks before braiding or storing.
sources: European Commission — EU Geographical Indications register, 'Taşköprü Sarımsağı' PGI registration
Turkish Patent and Trademark Office — geographically indicated products registry

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container vines in early spring on a trellis in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Kalecik Karası is native to a semi-arid continental climate and needs a long, warm growing season to ripen fully.

directions: Kalecik Karası is a native Turkish red wine grape named for the town of Kalecik near Ankara, where it was nearly lost to cultivation before agricultural researchers helped revive it in the late twentieth century into the backbone of Turkey's modern quality red wine industry. The thin-skinned berries give light-to-medium-bodied wines with pale ruby color, low tannin, and bright red-fruit aromatics of sour cherry, raspberry, and strawberry that have drawn comparisons to Pinot Noir or Gamay, while also working well for rosé and traditional-method sparkling wine. Train vines on a sturdy trellis in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, and expect strong vigor that benefits from canopy management to maintain fruit quality and air circulation. It ripens in the long, hot-but-not-extreme summers and cool nights typical of the Anatolian plateau, and shows good tolerance of the region's dry conditions once established.
sources: Club Oenologique — Turkish wine: Getting to know Turkey's indigenous grapes
The Guide Istanbul — Know what you drink: popular grape varieties in Turkey

common_name: Picholine Marocaine Olive (Morocco's Dominant Dual-Purpose Olive)

planting.note: Plant grafted or container trees in early spring in well-drained, calcareous soil in full sun; Picholine Marocaine is only partially self-compatible and sets a more reliable crop with a second cultivar nearby.

directions: Picholine Marocaine is, despite its French-sounding name, a distinct Moroccan landrace cultivar that dominates the country's olive growing, occupying the vast majority of its traditional orchards from coastal plains to arid pre-Saharan zones. It is a true dual-purpose variety, pressed for oil with an unusually high oleic acid content prized for stability and mild, balanced flavor, or brine-cured green for table olives, and its broad climatic adaptability has made it the backbone cultivar of Moroccan olive agriculture for generations. Plant grafted trees in well-drained, calcareous soil in full sun, where its deep rooting and good drought tolerance suit regions with hot, dry summers once the tree is established. Harvest green in early fall for table-olive curing or let fruit darken further into winter for the highest-quality oil pressing, and expect medium-sized fruit that sheds somewhat readily from the tree as it ripens.
sources: International Olive Council — World Olive Catalogue, Picholine Marocaine variety profile
PMC — Characterization of Phenolic Compounds, Vitamin E and Fatty Acids from Monovarietal Virgin Olive Oils of 'Picholine marocaine' Cultivar

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring once all frost danger has passed, into deep, sandy or calcareous, very well-drained soil in full sun; argan is slow-growing and extremely drought-tolerant but has almost no tolerance for freezing temperatures or waterlogged ground.

directions: Argan is a slow-growing, thorny, long-lived evergreen tree endemic to the semi-arid Souss Valley and surrounding regions of southwestern Morocco, where its hard-shelled fruit yields the kernels pressed into prized culinary and cosmetic argan oil. Traditional harvest relies on fruit that has fallen and partially dried on the ground, which is then cracked by hand to extract the oil-rich kernel inside, a labor-intensive process that has long supported women's cooperatives in the species' native range. Plant in full sun on sandy, calcareous, extremely well-drained soil and water only sparingly once established, since argan is adapted to some of the driest, hottest growing conditions of any commercially valuable fruiting tree and resents both winter wet and any hint of frost. Seedlings are notoriously slow to establish and trees may take a decade or more before bearing a meaningful crop, so argan is best approached as a long-term planting in genuinely frost-free, arid-to-semi-arid gardens.
sources: PFAF (Plants For A Future) Plant Database — Argania spinosa
Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Argania spinosa

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Bayoudhi is a common, self-fruitful oasis fig from the arid interior of Tunisia and does not require caprification to set fruit.

directions: Bayoudhi is a traditional Tunisian fig cultivar long grown in oasis plantings such as the Gafsa region of central Tunisia, where its light green to pale orange-skinned fruit is valued especially for drying rather than fresh eating, producing a tangy, concentrated dried fig distinct from sweeter commercial types. Researchers studying it among several old local fig genotypes have noted its notably high acidity and strong antioxidant pigment content compared with neighboring cultivars, qualities that carry through into the dried product and its traditional use in fruit infusions. Grow it the same way as other common-type figs, in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with minimal winter pruning, and expect good tolerance of the hot, arid, oasis-margin conditions of its native range once roots are established. Harvest as fruit softens and begins to sag on the stem, then sun-dry on racks for the traditional preserved product this cultivar is best known for.
sources: ScienceDirect — Physiological traits, fruit morphology and biochemical performance of six old fig genotypes grown in warm climates 'Gafsa oasis' in Tunisia
ResearchGate — Assessment of Genetic Diversity among Some Southern Tunisian Fig (Ficus carica L.) Cultivars Based on Morphological Descriptors

common_name: Boufeggous Date Palm (Tafilalet Moroccan Soft Date)

planting.note: Plant rooted offshoots in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing palms widely; Boufeggous is one of the most commonly planted date cultivars across Moroccan oases and tolerates the saline, mineral-heavy irrigation water typical of those regions better than many other date cultivars.

directions: Boufeggous is one of the most widely grown date palm cultivars across Moroccan oases, especially in the Tafilalet region, valued by farmers for its reliability, good salt tolerance, and a dark brown, soft-textured fruit that is notably larger and heavier than classic Deglet Noor dates. Its high sugar and potassium content give it an intensely sweet flavor and make it a dietary staple in the date-growing communities of southeastern Morocco, where it is eaten fresh off the tree during the harvest season rather than cured and stored long-term like drier commercial dates. Plant offshoots in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with regular irrigation through the oasis-style flood or drip systems traditional to Moroccan date culture, and expect female palms to need a male pollinator or hand pollination to set a reliable crop. Boufeggous shows good relative tolerance of the saline soil and irrigation water common to Moroccan oasis agriculture compared with more sensitive date cultivars.
sources: ResearchGate — Quantitative and Qualitative Characterization of 'Boufeggous' Dates (Phoenix dactylifera L.): A Comparative Analysis from Different Provinces in Southeast Morocco
Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations — date palm germplasm records, North Africa
